scenes.text: A travel graph turns a journey into shapes, choose positive, split the story into phases and add their durations to mark key times. Choose each phases shape, label axis and units, then mark key values and sign changes.

Read the verbs as drawing instructions steadily gives a horizontal velocity line, uniformly slows gives a straight slope to zero, weights sits on the axis, returns belongs below zero because a way is positive, add durations, the phase times are cumulative

Displacement time gradient gives velocity. Steeper means faster. Velocity time height must match that gradient at the same instant. Going back, accumulate signed areas from the starting displacement. Positive area adds, negative area subtracts. Now use that bridge to build both graphs for this lift.

Consider a lift that starts from rest. Accelerates at 1 .5 metres per second squared for two seconds, cruises for four seconds, then breaks to a stop in two seconds. Upwards positive. Let's get drawing. What speed? Velocity equals initial velocity plus acceleration times time. V equals u plus a t. Three metres per second. When does cruising end? Six seconds. When does it stop? Eight seconds. What displacement does each area give? Displacement equals area under the velocity time graph. S equals half u plus v times t. First triangle? Three metres. The rectangle? Twelve metres. Accumulated height? Fifteen metres. Braking adds? Three metres. Still upwards. Where does it finish? Eighteen metres above the start.

scenes.text: Positive velocity makes displacement rise. Zero velocity makes it level. Negative velocity makes it fall. On the return, velocity is negative, but displacement remains positive until the traveler reaches the start. Keep the whole return leg. Arriving back does not erase it.

Consider a ball thrown straight up at 15 metres per second. It goes up, stops, comes back down. Displacement is zero back at the start. Distance counts up and down. Vector versus scalar. Okay, enough chatter. Let's get drawing. Why a straight velocity line? Velocity equals initial velocity plus acceleration times time. V equals u plus a t. Gravity is ten downwards. V equals fifteen minus ten t. Where does direction change? At zero velocity, 1 .5 seconds. How high? Displacement equals area under the velocity -time graph. S equals half u plus v, times t. Eleven point two five metres. When back at hand height, three seconds equal signed areas cancel. What velocity then? Minus 15 metres per second. What if thrown faster? Higher, longer, same gradient.

scenes.text: A sketch needs correct shapes, signs, and phase order. An accurate plot also needs calculated, coordinates, and consistent scale. Check both for labeled axes, units, key time, and value. Show the negative region whenever motion reverses.

Consider a cyclist who leaves a, cruises away, slows to a stop, rests, then returns to a. Now the displacement time graph. Gradient equals displacement change over time change. V equals delta s over delta t. Cruising? What slope? 12 metres in four seconds, positive three. Slowing? What change? Three metres in two seconds. Positive slope flattens. Called? Average velocity. Resting? What slope? Zero metres in three seconds, zero gradient. Returning? What sign? Minus fifteen metres in five seconds. Negative three. Now the velocity time graph. Cruising? Positive three, horizontal. Slowing? Straight down to zero. Resting? Zero along the axis. Returning? Minus three, below zero. The jump idealises turning.
